questions.q: How does the cutover plan differ from the Lesson 8 runbook?
options: They're the same document presented twice
The runbook answers how the system works and how to operate it; the cutover plan answers when to switch and what happens if it goes wrong
The cutover plan replaces the need for a resource inventory entirely
The runbook is only for Priya, and the cutover plan is only for Theo
questions.explain: They answer different questions for different moments -- ongoing operation versus the specific decision of whether and when to go live.

questions.q: Why does the cutover plan specify a short DNS TTL set in advance of the actual switch?
options: Short TTLs are required by Azure for all storage accounts
So the DNS change propagates quickly once cutover happens, instead of staying cached on some visitors' devices for hours
TTL only affects email delivery, not web traffic
A short TTL prevents the alert rule from firing during cutover
questions.explain: Setting a short TTL ahead of time means the DNS change that actually redirects customer traffic takes effect quickly across visitors, rather than being delayed by cached records.

questions.q: Why must the rollback trigger be decided before cutover, rather than in the moment something goes wrong?
options: Because Azure CLI commands cannot be run during an active incident
Because deciding it calmly in advance avoids inventing a threshold while customers are already seeing errors, which is exactly the situation a pre-agreed trigger is meant to prevent
Because rollback is technically impossible once cutover has started
Because Priya is the only person allowed to approve a rollback
questions.explain: A rollback trigger agreed on beforehand means there's no debate needed in the moment -- the whole point is removing decision-making pressure from an active incident.

questions.q: What does "headline-first" communication mean in the context of presenting this plan to Priya?
options: Only presenting good news and omitting any risks
Stating the actual ask -- approve this date and this rollback trigger -- in the first thirty seconds, with supporting detail available if asked, rather than building up to it after lengthy background
Using technical jargon to establish credibility first
Reading the full resource inventory table before stating anything else
questions.explain: Priya needs to hear the actual decision being requested immediately; everything else is detail she can ask about afterward if she wants it.

questions.q: What is the correct response if Priya asks about a scenario genuinely outside this project's scope, like an Azure-wide outage during cutover?
options: Confidently improvise a plausible-sounding answer on the spot
Say plainly that it's a real scenario outside this Beginner project's scope, worth flagging as a future question rather than guessing
Change the subject to avoid the question
Claim the scenario is impossible and cannot occur
questions.explain: A stakeholder trusts an honest "that's out of scope, here's why" far more than a confident guess that wasn't actually validated.
